conventional_description:
In Western medicine, nausea is defined as an unpleasant sensation of unease and discomfort in the upper stomach with an involuntary urge to vomit. It is not a disease itself but a symptom that can arise from a wide range of causes: gastrointestinal disorders (gastritis, gastroenteritis, reflux), neurological conditions (migraine, vestibular dysfunction), metabolic disturbances (pregnancy, uremia), medications (chemotherapy, opioids), or even psychological factors (anxiety).
Diagnosis relies on a detailed history - onset, triggers, associated symptoms - and may be supported by physical examination, lab tests, or imaging when an underlying condition is suspected. Acute nausea often resolves on its own or with short-term medication, while chronic nausea (lasting more than a month) can be more challenging to manage and may require investigation for functional disorders like functional dyspepsia or cyclic vomiting syndrome.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment typically begins with dietary modifications (small, bland meals; avoidance of triggers) and over-the-counter or prescription antiemetics. Common medications include antihistamines (dimenhydrinate, meclizine), dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide), serotonin antagonists (ondansetron), and anticholinergics (scopolamine). For nausea related to specific conditions - such as migraine, pregnancy, or chemotherapy - targeted protocols exist. In chronic cases, prokinetic agents or neuromodulators (low-dose tricyclic antidepressants) may be used to modulate gut-brain signaling.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, all nausea is understood as a form of rebellious Stomach Qi. The Stomach is designed to send food and Qi downward; when something disrupts that downward movement, Qi rises instead, producing the sensation of nausea and the urge to vomit. The question is never “is there rebellious Qi?” but “what is causing the rebellion?”
The answer often involves more than just the Stomach. The Liver is a frequent culprit: its job is to keep Qi flowing smoothly throughout the body, and when emotional stress or frustration causes Liver Qi to stagnate, it can attack the Stomach horizontally, pushing Qi upward. The Spleen is equally important - it transforms food and fluids into usable energy, and when it is weak (from poor diet, overwork, or constitutional tendency), it fails to manage fluids, leading to the accumulation of phlegm or dampness that obstructs the Stomach and triggers nausea.
External pathogens can also invade suddenly - a blast of cold weather, for instance, can penetrate the digestive system and congeal Qi, causing acute nausea with chills and abdominal pain. And when the Stomach's own resources are depleted - whether its warming Yang or its moistening Yin - the organ loses the ability to ripen food and send Qi downward, producing a chronic, low-grade nausea that feels very different from the acute kind.
This is why two people with the same Western diagnosis of “chronic nausea” may receive completely different TCM treatments. One may need to soothe an angry Liver, another to clear a backlog of undigested food, and a third to warm a cold, depleted Stomach. The treatment fits the pattern, not the symptom label.

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner starts by asking when the nausea started, what brings it on, and what it feels like. The quality and timing are the first clues that separate one pattern from another. A sudden onset that follows a chill or a heavy meal tells a very different story than a slow, nagging queasiness that has been around for months and flares with stress.
If the nausea is accompanied by sour belching, acid reflux, and a distended feeling in the sides of the ribcage, and especially if it worsens with emotional upset, the picture points to Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach. The tongue edges may look redder than the rest, and the pulse often feels tight and wiry.
When nausea strikes after overeating or indulging in rich, greasy food, Food Stagnation in the Stomach is the likely culprit. The person will describe a foul, sour taste in the mouth, loud belching, and a bloated, heavy sensation in the upper belly. The tongue coating becomes thick and greasy, and the pulse feels slippery under the fingers.
A queasy feeling with a sensation of sloshing water in the stomach, a heavy head, and perhaps some dizziness suggests Phlegm‑Fluids in the Stomach and Small Intestine. The nausea may produce watery spit‑up, and the person often feels worse after drinking liquids. The tongue has a white, greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery.
An acute, sudden wave of nausea that arrives with chills, a low‑grade fever, body aches, and a headache points to an Exterior Cold invading the Interior. This pattern usually follows exposure to cold or wind. The tongue coating is thin and white, and the pulse floats at the surface, as if the body is trying to push the invader out.
When nausea has been intermittent for a long time, comes with a poor appetite, and the person feels cold in the hands and feet, Stomach Yang Deficient and Cold is at play. Warm drinks and a hot water bottle bring relief, while cold foods make it worse. The tongue looks pale and the pulse is deep and weak. If instead the nausea is a dry heaving with a parched mouth and throat, and the tongue is red with little coating, the pattern is Stomach Yin Deficiency, where the stomach lacks the fluids to moisten and descend.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach
patterns.symptoms: ["Nausea triggered or worsened by stress or frustration", "Acid reflux or sour regurgitation", "Distending pain in the upper abdomen that radiates to the ribs", "Frequent belching and sighing", "Irritability and moodiness"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and frustration, Anger or arguments, Greasy, fried, or heavy foods, Alcohol, Irregular eating
patterns.better_with: Emotional calm and relaxation, Gentle movement or stretching, Warm, easily digested foods like congee, Deep breathing or meditation
patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress, frustration, or anger causes Liver Qi to stagnate. The Liver channel runs through the chest and ribs, and when its Qi is stuck, it can attack the Stomach, disrupting its normal downward movement. The Stomach Qi then rebels upward, producing nausea along with acid reflux, belching, and a feeling of fullness in the upper abdomen that often radiates to the ribs.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body, redder on the sides, thin white coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string, most pronounced at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and frustration cause Liver Qi to stagnate, which then attacks the Stomach, so emotional calm directly reduces the root cause of the nausea. Gentle movement helps Qi flow, while heavy, greasy foods and alcohol burden the Stomach and worsen stagnation, making the Qi rebel upward more forcefully.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Manage stress with gentle daily movement like walking, yoga, or tai chi. Eat small, warm meals at regular times, and avoid cold, raw, or greasy foods that burden the Stomach. Deep breathing or meditation can help keep Liver Qi flowing smoothly.

patterns.symptoms: ["Nausea after eating, often with sour or rotten belching", "Upper abdominal bloating and pain that worsens with pressure", "Vomiting of sour, undigested food, which temporarily relieves the discomfort", "Thick, greasy, curd-like coating on the tongue, thickest in the centre", "Aversion to food and its smell", "Foul-smelling flatulence or loose stools with a sour odour"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating or eating too quickly, Greasy, fried, or heavy foods, Cold, raw, or dairy foods, Eating late at night, Lying down right after eating
patterns.better_with: Eating lightly or skipping a meal, Vomiting (temporarily clears the blockage), Warm, easily digested foods like congee, Gentle abdominal massage
patterns.why_this_happens: When you eat too much, too quickly, or consume foods that are heavy and greasy, your Stomach's normal downward movement can become overwhelmed. Undigested food simply sits there and begins to ferment, creating a blockage that forces Stomach Qi to rebel upward instead of descending. That rebellion is what you feel as nausea, often accompanied by sour, rotten-smelling belches as the stagnant food putrefies.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Body is usually normal in colour and shape, but the coating is thick, greasy, and curd-like, thickest in the centre. Pulse: Slippery (滑, Huá), full and replete, especially prominent at the right middle (Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating and rich foods create a physical backlog that the Stomach cannot process, causing Qi to rebel upward as nausea. Vomiting temporarily expels the stagnant matter, which is why it brings relief. Light, warm foods like congee are easy to digest and gently support Spleen Qi without adding to the burden. Fasting or eating less gives the Stomach the time and space it needs to clear the accumulation and restore its normal downward movement. Gentle abdominal massage encourages peristalsis and helps move stagnant food along.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, lighter meals and avoid greasy, fried, dairy, and cold foods until your appetite and digestion return. A short fast or a day of plain congee can give your Stomach the break it needs to process the backlog. Chew each mouthful thoroughly, and take a gentle walk after eating rather than sitting or lying down.

patterns.pattern_name: Phlegm-Fluids in the Stomach and Small intestine
patterns.symptoms: ["Vomiting of clear, watery fluid", "Splashing or gurgling sound in the stomach (with movement or tapping)", "No thirst, or thirst without desire to drink", "Dizziness and lightheadedness", "Feeling of heaviness in the body"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw, or dairy foods, Greasy, fried, or heavy foods, Drinking large amounts of water, Damp, humid weather, Lying down right after eating
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the abdomen, Warm ginger tea, Gentle movement or stretching, Rest
patterns.why_this_happens: When Spleen Yang is weak, it can no longer transform and transport fluids properly. These unprocessed fluids accumulate into pathological Phlegm-Fluids that settle in the Stomach. The stagnant fluids obstruct the Stomach's downward movement, causing Qi to rebel upward as nausea, often with vomiting of thin, watery fluid. The sloshing fluids also produce a characteristic gurgling sound and a heavy, bloated sensation in the upper abdomen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, white slippery coating, excessively moist. Pulse: deep (Chen), wiry (Xian), and slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold, raw, and greasy foods further weaken Spleen Yang and generate Dampness, adding to the phlegm-fluid accumulation that disrupts the Stomach's descent. Warmth and ginger tea directly warm the Middle Burner, helping to transform and move stagnant fluids so Qi can descend. Gentle movement encourages the flow of Qi and fluids, while lying down after eating allows fluids to stagnate.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee and soups, and avoid cold, raw, or greasy items that create Dampness. Sip warm ginger tea to help transform fluids. Keep the abdomen wrapped or use a warm compress to support Spleen Yang.

patterns.better_with: Warmth on the abdomen, Warm drinks and soups, Warm ginger tea, Rest, Moxibustion on the navel
patterns.why_this_happens: When an intense external Cold pathogen penetrates directly into the interior, it congeals the body's Yang and freezes the normal flow of Qi. The Stomach, which depends on warmth and downward movement to function, becomes a pool of cold stagnant energy. Its Qi rebels upward instead of descending, producing nausea and the vomiting of clear, watery fluid.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, and teeth-marked body with a white, moist, slippery coating. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), slow (迟 chí), or tight (紧 jǐn).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold is a congealing force that freezes Yang and paralyzes the Stomach's ability to move Qi downward. This causes Qi to rebel upward as nausea. Warmth counteracts Cold by restoring the flow of Yang, relaxing the constricted vessels, and allowing the Stomach to resume its natural descending motion. Ginger and moxibustion directly infuse the middle burner with heat, stopping the rebellion at its root.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the abdomen warm and avoid all cold or raw foods and iced drinks. Sip warm ginger tea or broth throughout the day. Eat small, warm, easily digested meals like congee with a pinch of dried ginger. Protect yourself from drafts and cold environments, and use a hot water bottle on the belly at the first sign of nausea.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach needs its Yang warmth to ripen food and send Qi downward. When that warmth is chronically deficient, internal Cold builds up, digestion slows, and Qi rebels upward instead of descending - producing intermittent nausea. The Cold also impairs fluid transformation, so you may vomit clear watery fluid, and the nausea tends to ease with warmth and light pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, puffy, and tender with teeth marks; white slippery coating. Pulse: Deep, slow, and weak, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Warmth directly supplements the deficient Stomach Yang, helping it descend Qi and stop the rebellion that causes nausea. Rest conserves Qi, while fatigue and cold drain what little Yang remains, making nausea worse. Heavy or raw foods overwhelm the already weak digestive fire, triggering nausea.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat only warm, cooked foods and avoid raw, cold, or greasy meals that tax the Stomach's warmth. Ginger tea or a pinch of dried ginger in congee can help settle nausea. Keep your abdomen warm with a compress or a warm water bottle, and avoid cold drinks and iced foods entirely.

patterns.better_with: Small sips of warm water or pear juice, Warm, easily digested foods like congee, Resting in a cool, quiet room, Deep breathing or meditation, Avoiding spicy and dry foods
patterns.why_this_happens:
Stomach Yin is the cooling, moistening fluid that keeps the stomach lining smooth and allows food to be properly broken down. When Yin runs low, the stomach becomes dry and overheated, like a pot boiling with too little water. The Stomach Qi, which should move downward, rebels upward instead, producing a dry, queasy sensation that often feels like a gnawing emptiness rather than bloating.
Without enough Yin to lubricate the digestive process, even small amounts of food can trigger nausea, and the person may feel hungry yet turned off by the thought of eating. The nausea tends to be a dry heaving with little or no vomit, accompanied by a parched mouth and throat.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body, dry in the center, with little or no coating and possible cracks. Pulse: fine (Xi) and rapid (Shu), especially weak at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Yin is like the cooling water that keeps the digestive fire from raging. Spicy, fried, and dry foods, as well as overwork and late nights, burn up that water, making the stomach even drier and more irritated, which triggers nausea. Small sips of fluids and moistening foods gently replenish Yin and soothe the stomach, while rest and cool surroundings prevent further Yin loss. Calming the mind helps because emotional stress can generate heat, which consumes Yin and stirs up rebellious Stomach Qi.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent meals of moistening, easy-to-digest foods like congee, pear, apple, and steamed vegetables. Avoid spicy, fried, dry, or heavily roasted foods that further consume Yin. Sip warm water or herbal teas (chrysanthemum, honeysuckle) throughout the day rather than drinking large amounts at once. Protect your Yin by going to bed early and avoiding overwork, long hours in front of screens, and intense exercise that leaves you drained.

faqs.question: How quickly can acupuncture relieve nausea?
faqs.answer: For acute nausea - from a stomach bug, a bad meal, or motion sickness - many patients feel significant relief during or immediately after the first acupuncture session. The point Neiguan (PC-6) on the inner wrist is especially fast-acting for settling rebellious Stomach Qi. For chronic or stress-related nausea, acupuncture works more gradually, with noticeable improvement usually after 3-5 weekly sessions as the underlying pattern begins to shift.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my anti-nausea medication?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes - but always inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about everything you are taking. Chinese herbs are generally gentle and work through different mechanisms than pharmaceutical antiemetics, so they can often be used alongside each other. Your TCM practitioner may adjust the timing (taking herbs and medications a few hours apart) to avoid any digestive interference. Never stop prescribed medication abruptly without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for nausea during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM has a long history of treating morning sickness safely, and acupuncture (especially PC-6) is well-studied for pregnancy-related nausea. However, certain herbs are contraindicated during pregnancy because they move Qi or Blood too strongly. Always see a licensed TCM practitioner who is experienced in prenatal care - they will select only pregnancy-safe points and formulas. Never self-prescribe herbs while pregnant.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I'm nauseous?
faqs.answer: From a TCM perspective, cold, raw, greasy, and overly sweet or spicy foods are the biggest culprits - they either chill the Stomach, create dampness, or overwhelm digestion, all of which can trigger rebellious Qi. Dairy, fried foods, iced drinks, and heavy meats are common offenders. Instead, favor warm, cooked, easily digested foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and ginger tea. Eating small, frequent meals rather than large portions also helps keep Stomach Qi moving downward.

faqs.question: Why does my nausea get worse when I'm stressed?
faqs.answer: Stress directly impacts the Liver, whose job in TCM is to ensure the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. When you're frustrated, anxious, or overwhelmed, Liver Qi stagnates and often “invades” the Stomach horizontally, disrupting its downward movement. This is why you may notice nausea paired with a tight sensation under the ribs, acid reflux, or belching during tense moments. Treating the Liver - with herbs, acupuncture, and stress management - is often the key to breaking this cycle.

faqs.question: Does TCM work for chronic nausea that has lasted for months?
faqs.answer: Yes, chronic nausea is one of the conditions where TCM can be particularly helpful because it addresses the constitutional weakness that conventional medicine often labels as “functional” or “idiopathic.” Whether the root is Spleen deficiency, phlegm accumulation, or Stomach Yin depletion, treatment aims to rebuild the digestive system's strength over time. Most patients with chronic nausea see gradual improvement over 4-8 weeks of consistent herbs and weekly acupuncture, with the nausea becoming less frequent and less intense before it disappears.

faqs.question: What does a TCM practitioner look for to diagnose my nausea?
faqs.answer: Your practitioner will ask detailed questions about the quality of your nausea: Is it a burning sensation or a heavy, sloshy feeling? Does it come with sour belching, a dry mouth, or a craving for warmth? They will also examine your tongue (looking at its color, shape, and coating) and feel your pulse at both wrists. These clues, combined with your emotional state, dietary habits, and medical history, allow them to identify which specific pattern is causing your nausea and tailor treatment accordingly.

faqs.question: Can children use TCM for nausea?
faqs.answer: Yes, children generally respond very well to TCM for nausea. Acupuncture is safe for children when performed by a practitioner experienced in pediatric care - needles are often retained for only a few seconds or replaced with non-insertive techniques like acupressure or laser acupuncture. Herbal formulas can be prescribed in reduced dosages or in forms like granules that are easier to take. Pediatric nausea often resolves more quickly than adult cases, sometimes within a few days.

research.title: Stimulation of the wrist acupuncture point PC6 for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting
research.description: Cochrane systematic review of 40 trials (4,858 participants) showing that PC6 stimulation significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting compared to sham treatment, with an effect similar to antiemetic drugs but fewer side effects.
research.periodical: Lee A, Fan LTY. Stimulation of the wrist acupuncture point PC6 for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2009, Issue 2. Art. No.: CD003281.

research.title: Ginger for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy: randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial
research.description: A double-blind RCT of 70 pregnant women with nausea found that 1 g of ginger daily for 4 days significantly reduced nausea severity and vomiting episodes compared to placebo, with no adverse effects on pregnancy outcomes.
research.periodical: Vutyavanich T, Kraisarin T, Ruangsri RA. Ginger for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy: randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial. Obstetrics & Gynecology 2001;97(4):577-82.

research.title: Acupuncture-point stimulation for chemotherapy-induced nausea or vomiting
research.description: Cochrane review of 11 RCTs (1,247 participants) demonstrating that electroacupuncture at PC6 reduced the incidence of acute vomiting after chemotherapy, while self-administered acupressure showed a protective effect for acute nausea.
research.periodical: Ezzo J, Richardson MA, Vickers A, et al. Acupuncture-point stimulation for chemotherapy-induced nausea or vomiting. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2006, Issue 2. Art. No.: CD002285.
